profiles.meeting_scenario: The HASE platform team is holding a planning meeting to prepare a fall-semester rollout of two human-factor features inspired by prior agile development research: a weekly morale check-in for Scrum teams and SMART-based task-assignment suggestions. The context is that one capstone course, CS405, wants to use the updated platform in six weeks, and faculty advisors have asked for better visibility into team health before the mid-semester review. The agenda is to decide the rollout scope for the CS405 pilot, what must be built in the next two sprints, how historical HASE data will be used to initialize the recommendation defaults, and who owns faculty-facing setup and monitoring pieces. The expected outcome is a shared plan for sprint deliverables, responsibilities, and a timeline for launching the pilot.

members.name: Nina Patel
members.expertise: Agile workflow design, faculty onboarding, student-facing product requirements
members.background: Former software engineering instructor who now works with university partners to adapt HASE for project-based courses and capstone programs.
members.private_state: She wants a visibly successful semester launch that faculty can use without extra coordination, and she is especially concerned that advisors can identify struggling teams early enough to intervene.
hidden_assumptions: When a course is named as the pilot, the expectation is that the whole course section uses the feature set consistently rather than a small opt-in subset.
A weekly morale check-in should align to the Scrum rhythm of the course, meaning students see it at the same point in the sprint cycle each week.
An advisor dashboard is only truly ready if it highlights at-risk teams clearly enough for faculty to act without manual interpretation.
Using last semester's HASE data means starting from the cleaned research dataset already prepared by the analytics group, not raw transactional logs.

members.name: Leo Chen
members.expertise: Backend systems, feature-flag rollouts, data pipelines, platform reliability
members.background: Full-stack engineer who has maintained HASE through several semester launches and prefers operationally conservative deployments with minimal support overhead.
members.private_state: He wants to reduce launch risk before the semester starts, avoid committing engineering work that depends on unstable data preparation, and keep the first release narrow enough for his small team to support.
hidden_assumptions: Calling something a pilot normally implies a feature-flagged beta with only a few volunteer teams before a broader course rollout.
A weekly check-in is best implemented as an automated every-seven-days workflow anchored to each user's first completed check-in because that matches the existing notification service.
A dashboard can be considered ready if advisors can open a page and inspect morale trends manually; explicit risk labeling can be added later.
Last semester's HASE data refers to the most recent production database tables, since those are the accessible source that matches the current schema.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to 'pilot this in CS405.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nina means the entire CS405 course section, including all student teams and all assigned faculty advisors, so the course experience is uniform.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leo means a limited beta inside CS405 with only three volunteer teams behind a feature flag before expanding further.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Naming the same course creates a strong feeling of agreement, and each assumes the usual organizational meaning of 'pilot' is obvious in their environment, so neither thinks to restate the inclusion boundary.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to add a 'weekly morale check-in.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nina expects one synchronized prompt per team each week, sent around the course's sprint cadence so advisors can compare morale snapshots across teams at the same time.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leo expects to implement the existing rolling notification pattern, where each student receives the prompt every seven days based on their own prior completion time.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'weekly' sounds fully precise in ordinary conversation, and cadence mechanics feel like an implementation detail neither side believes needs special clarification during a planning discussion.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as advisor dashboard ready
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the 'advisor dashboard' needs to be ready before the mid-semester review.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nina means advisors should see automatically flagged at-risk teams, trend summaries, and an easy way to scan multiple teams before review meetings.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leo means a basic page showing each team's morale and workload trend lines is sufficient, even if advisors must interpret risk manually and no cross-team summary exists yet.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both sincerely want the dashboard available by the same date, and 'ready' feels like a shared milestone term even though each silently applies a different threshold for completeness.

misalignment_points.topic: Which historical data will seed SMART defaults
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to 'use last semester's HASE data' to initialize recommendation defaults.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nina is thinking of the curated Spring 2024 research dataset that the analytics group cleaned for prior human-factor analysis and that excludes incomplete team records.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leo is thinking of the raw Spring 2024 production event tables in the operational database because they are directly available to engineering and fit current ETL jobs.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'last semester's data' appears specific enough to both of them, and each assumes there is one canonical recent dataset, so the referential gap remains invisible.

turns.inner_thought: We have six weeks, so I need a clean commitment now. If CS405 is the pilot, that needs to mean the whole section uses the new flow, not a side experiment with a few teams. Faculty will not want two different student experiences in one course, and I definitely do not want extra coordination overhead during launch.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I want to use this to lock the plan for piloting the new morale and task-assignment work in CS405 before semester kickoff, so we leave today with clear sprint targets and owners.

turns.inner_thought: Six weeks is tight but manageable if we keep the CS405 pilot narrow and reversible. I do not want to promise a course-wide rollout on first release; three volunteer teams behind a flag is the kind of pilot we can actually support without blowing up launch week.
turns.utterance: That should be workable from engineering's side if we keep the CS405 pilot controlled and sequence things carefully across the next two sprints.

turns.inner_thought: The faculty message has been consistent: they want a weekly morale check-in that lines up with the course sprint rhythm, and they need the advisor dashboard ready before the mid-semester review in a way that makes struggling teams obvious at a glance. If advisors still have to interpret everything manually, they'll miss intervention windows.
turns.utterance: From the faculty side, the two big asks are pretty clear: a weekly morale check-in for students, and an advisor dashboard they can rely on before the mid-semester review.

turns.inner_thought: Good, the weekly morale check-in maps well to the notification service we already have. We can trigger it every seven days per user based on when they last completed one, which saves us from building a separate scheduler. That's the fastest path and keeps support simple.
turns.utterance: For the weekly morale check-in, I'd like to reuse the existing notification service so we can get it out quickly without introducing a lot of new infrastructure.

turns.inner_thought: As long as the weekly morale check-in is in place on the course cadence, advisors should be able to compare teams side by side each week and see who is drifting before review meetings. The dashboard has to surface that clearly enough that faculty can act without spending time decoding charts.
turns.utterance: Yes, and once the weekly check-in is live, I want advisors to be able to scan who is drifting and step in ahead of those course review meetings.

turns.inner_thought: I can get the advisor dashboard ready before the mid-semester review if we keep the first cut basic: a page with team-level morale and workload trends. That counts as ready to me. Risk flags and cross-team summaries are useful, but those are follow-on polish if we have time.
turns.utterance: I think the advisor dashboard can be ready in time if we treat the first version as a solid baseline with team-level trends, and then leave some polish for the following sprint.

turns.inner_thought: On the SMART side, we should absolutely use last semester's HASE data, meaning the cleaned analytics dataset from Spring 2024. That gives us realistic defaults without the noise from incomplete records. I do not want recommendations seeded from messy raw data and then have faculty lose trust right away.
turns.utterance: Great. On the SMART setup, I also think we should use last semester's HASE data to seed the initial recommendation defaults so the pilot starts from realistic patterns.

turns.inner_thought: That's straightforward if we use the Spring production tables. They're already accessible, match the current schema, and fit the ETL jobs we have. I do not want this sprint blocked waiting on somebody else's curated dataset or cleanup work.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I can have one of the engineers pull last semester's HASE data from the existing production tables, which should let us initialize that piece without blocking the sprint.

turns.inner_thought: Okay, then I'll own faculty coordination and frame this as the CS405 pilot for the fall setup across the course once the weekly check-ins and advisor dashboard are in place. Faculty advisors should be able to use it directly without me doing constant interpretation or special-case rollout management.
turns.utterance: That works. I'll take the faculty coordination piece and line up the CS405 pilot as part of the fall setup once the dashboard and check-ins are in place.

turns.inner_thought: Good. Engineering can proceed with a narrow pilot rollout in CS405, wire up the weekly morale workflow using the existing cadence logic, ship a basic dashboard page before the review point, and import the recent production data for SMART defaults. That keeps risk contained and gives us something supportable in time.
turns.utterance: Perfect. I'll break out engineering work for the pilot rollout in CS405, the weekly morale workflow, the advisor dashboard page, and the historical-data import, and we'll start sprint planning against that this afternoon.
